title: 3 friends complete 8,000-km canoe journey across Canada, arriving in Vancouver
summary: After more than 200 days, thousands of kilometres and countless hours on the water, three longtime friends from Toronto completed their cross-Canada canoe journey on Sunday at Vancouver's Jericho…

image.caption: From front to back, Will Vyse, Georges Kirijian, and Nolan Aziz arrive at Jericho Beach in Vancouver on Sunday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

After more than 200 days, thousands of kilometres and countless hours on the water, three longtime friends from Toronto completed their cross-Canada canoe journey on Sunday at Vancouver's Jericho Beach.
Trio spent 219 days travelling through 6 provinces to raise money for northern, remote Indigenous communities

Nolan Aziz, Will Vyse and Georges Kirijian, all 24, received a warm welcome from family, friends and supporters who gathered near the Jericho Sailing Centre to celebrate the end of their 8,000-kilometre expedition.
The crowd cheered as the trio stepped ashore, with some supporters breaking into a rendition of O Canada.
The three men set out from Tadoussac, Que., in April as part of their canoe expedition, travelling through six provinces along rivers and lakes, often far from major cities.

items: Paddling across Canada one waterway at a time.

blocks.text: “I wanted to take the more unconventional route because I am very deeply fascinated with being the first to do something or trying something new…it’s deeply enthralling in a way,” Vyes told CBC News.
"There's a lot of magic in all the tiny hidden creeks and rivers that are out of the way that no one goes to.”
The trio believe they have completed the longest single-season canoe expedition ever recorded at more than 200 days.
From left to right, Nolan Aziz, Georges Kirijian, and Will Vys stand together while spectators sing O Canada during their arrival to Jericho beach in Vancouver. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

They previously finished a 60-day trip in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and decided to see if they could push that further and travel across the country in support of Truth North Aid, a charity that helps northern and remote Indigenous communities.
Their goal is to raise $1 million for the charity, and so far have raised just over $130,000.
Journey with plenty of challenges
The expedition was not without difficulties.
The trio paddled long distances each day, camped outdoors almost every night and sometimes had to carry their canoe over land when waterways became impassable.
Vyse said cold weather in Quebec delayed their progress, forcing them to carry their canoe for weeks while waiting for frozen lakes to thaw.
"We had to portage for like three weeks straight because the lakes just weren't thawing," he said.
The red canoe used by the three friends to complete their journey rests on Vancouver's Jericho Beach. (CBC)
Some portages stretched between 50 and 80 kilometres.
In B.C., the group faced a lengthy detour to avoid the dangerous currents of Hells Gate on the Fraser River.
They also encountered stormy weather and a bear near one of their campsites.
Kirijian said travelling in a single canoe meant they had to make careful decisions about safety.

items: Cross-Canada canoe journey raising funds for remote northern and Indigenous communities

blocks.text: "We're one canoe, we're three guys. We can't have any redundancy when it comes to any kinds of accidents in the water," he said. “We're always just going into things knowing we just have one boat, we cannot [be] rescued.”
But the journey also offered memorable experiences and some powerful insights, said Vyes.
“I think people are a lot better than we realize. Strangers are just friends we haven’t made yet,” he added.
Connections along the way
Among those welcoming the trio to Vancouver was Peatr Thomas, who travelled from Manitoba for their final landing.
Thomas met the paddlers when they stopped in his community during the 150-year-commemoration of the Bloodvein River First Nation's treaty signing.
He said the group showed an interest in learning about Indigenous communities and their relationship with the land and water.
The trio of canoeists were greeted by family with hugs and tears following their final landing. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)
"They also just wanted to know the perspective of the Indigenous peoples and the history and how we sort of connect with the land and the water as well," Thomas said.
Aziz said travelling across the country helped him appreciate the connections between Canadians from different regions and backgrounds.
“What we really saw, despite all the microcosms of different cultures that we have in this country ... we all have this shared national identity as Canadians and it's really beautiful,” he said.
With files from Ali Pitargue and The Canadian Press
